docs.title: What is fjc-biographies?
docs.text: fjc-biographies downloads the Federal Judicial Center's Biographical Directory of Article III Federal Judges and turns it into tidy tables, including a roster of judges in two formats: by appointment (a row for each court that each judge has served on) and by judge (a row for each judge).

docs.title: Why use fjc-biographies?
docs.text:
• One step. fjc-biographies downloads all six of the FJC's files (demographics, federal judicial service, other federal judicial service, education, professional career, and other nominations) and exports a tidy CSV file of each.
  • A roster of judges. build_roster codes what researchers usually want to know about each appointment: the circuit, the years of service and senior status, the appointing president's party, the ABA rating, the share of senators who voted to confirm, whether it was a recess appointment, the judge's gender and race, etc.
  • Fields from careers, written in a spreadsheet. A rulebook (a CSV file of regular expressions) makes new fields from each judge's employment history. The built-in "judges" rulebook flags whether the judge was a prosecutor, public defender, law clerk, Supreme Court clerk, solicitor general, or law professor, and your own rulebook can add flags, counts, labels, or lists of matches without changing any code. The employment history itself stays in the roster as career, one position per line, so every field can be checked against the text it was made from.
  • Names for matching. Each judge's name is written twelve ways, for matching it against opinions and other datasets: first, middle, and last names; with the middle initial; without the middle name; each with and without the suffix ("Milton Dale Smith, Jr."); and, for the FJC's names with letters in square brackets, both with the brackets removed ("Robert Lanier Anderson") and with the bracketed letters replaced by a period ("R. Lanier Anderson").
  • Ideology scores, if you want them. --jcs adds each appointment's Judicial Common Space score, computed by judicial-common-space, and --martin-quinn adds the justices' Martin-Quinn scores for each appointment to the Supreme Court and exports every justice's score in every term.
  • Reassignments handled. A judge who was reassigned to another court without a new appointment (as when the Eleventh Circuit was divided from the Fifth) keeps the president, party, rating, and vote of the judge's last appointment.

The roster is the one that courtpy uses to identify the judges of cases, which this package was taken from.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: Python 3.11 or later. The dependencies are pandas (3.0 or later), numpy, and judicial-common-space (0.1.0 or later), which pip installs with it.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
To install fjc-biographies, use pip:

pip install fjc-biographies

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
From the command line, download the files and export the tidy tables and the roster:

fjc-biographies

The roster is exported in two formats, as the FJC's own export is:

File Rows Columns roster_by_appointment.csv One for each court that each judge has served on The judge's fields, repeated on each of the judge's rows, and the appointment's fields (court, start_date, president, party, ...) roster_by_judge.csv One for each judge The judge's fields once, appointments (how many courts the judge has served on), and each appointment's fields, numbered in the order of the judge's service (court_1, start_date_1, ..., court_2, ...)

The FJC updates the directory nightly. Add --update to download the files again, --download-only to skip exporting, and --data-folder to choose where the files go. By default, they go in data/courts/fjc_biographies beside the folder of the repository, or in the user's application data folder when the package is installed (set FJC_BIOGRAPHIES_DATA_DIR to choose another).

From Python:

import fjc_biographies

# The tidy table of one file, which is downloaded if it is not there.
service = fjc_biographies.load('service')

# Every file, and the roster made from them.
tables = fjc_biographies.load_all()
roster = fjc_biographies.build_roster(
    tables['service'], tables['demographics'], tables['career'])

# The same roster with a row for each judge.
by_judge = fjc_biographies.roster_by_judge(roster)

To make other fields from judges' careers, copy the built-in rulebook (judges.csv), change or add rules, and name it:

roster = fjc_biographies.build_roster(
    tables['service'], tables['demographics'], tables['career'],
    rulebook = 'my_careers.csv')
careers = fjc_biographies.code_careers(tables['career'], rulebook = 'my_careers.csv')

or fjc-biographies --rulebook my_careers.csv from the command line. The columns of a rulebook and the kinds of rules are described in the instructions folder.

docs.title: Scores
docs.text:
Judicial Common Space and Martin-Quinn scores are optional:

fjc-biographies --jcs --martin-quinn

roster = fjc_biographies.add_jcs(roster)
roster = fjc_biographies.add_martin_quinn(roster)
terms = fjc_biographies.martin_quinn_terms()
Column Meaning jcs The appointment's Judicial Common Space score: the NOMINATE score of the judge's home-state senators of the president's party, or else of the president, and for a justice, the Martin-Quinn score of the appointment's first term on the same scale. mq_first, mq_last, mq_mean, mq_terms For an appointment to the Supreme Court, the justice's Martin-Quinn scores in its first and last terms, their mean, and the number of terms scored. A justice who became Chief Justice has separate scores for each appointment.

With --martin-quinn, martin_quinn_terms.csv has every justice's score in every term, with the FJC's nid and the appointment's sequence.

The files that the scores come from (Voteview's NOMINATE scores, the dates of senators' service, and the Martin-Quinn scores) are downloaded into judicial-common-space's data folder, which --scores-folder or the JUDICIAL_COMMON_SPACE_DATA_DIR environment variable can change, so that courtpy and judicial-common-space share them. The Martin-Quinn website sometimes refuses or fails to answer automated requests. Then save justices.csv from its page in a browser and pass its path: --martin-quinn ~/Downloads/justices.csv. A copy that was downloaded before is used if a new one cannot be.

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text: All notable changes to this project will be documented in this file.

• Exports the roster in two formats: by appointment (roster_by_appointment.csv, which was roster.csv) and by judge (roster_by_judge.csv, made by roster_by_judge), and run returns them as "roster_by_appointment" and "roster_by_judge".
  • Keeps each judge's professional career in the roster as career, one position per line, beside the fields made from it.
  • Writes each judge's name in twelve ways for matching (name_first_middle_last and the rest), with the FJC's bracketed letters removed or replaced by a period.
  • Adds the FJC's sequence of each appointment to the roster.
  • Adds optional Judicial Common Space scores (add_jcs, --jcs), computed by judicial-common-space (0.1.0 or later, from PyPI), and the justices' Martin-Quinn scores (add_martin_quinn, martin_quinn_terms, --martin-quinn).
  • The tests save the roster of their invented judges in both formats in tests/output, to be looked at.
  • Adds a citation file and a BibTeX citation in the README.

• Downloads the six files of the FJC's Biographical Directory of Article III Federal Judges, parses them into tidy tables, and builds a roster of each judge's service on each court (taken from courtpy.judges.build_roster).
  • Makes fields from judges' professional careers with courtpy's rules engine and its "judges" rulebook (instructions/judges.csv), or a rulebook of the user's own (rulebook and --rulebook).
  • Adds the fjc-biographies command.

docs.title: Style Guidelines
docs.text:
This package follows the Google Python Style Guide with two notable exceptions:

  1. It always adds spaces around "=". This not only violates the Google guide, it violates PEP8, the foundational Python style guide from which all other resources are derived. I defy this strong, long-standing norm because I find it more readable. My brain and eyes have trouble seeing two separate objects when an equal sign is in the middle. I imagine that I am not alone in this accessibility issue. Further, as PEP8 itself notes, required spaces around equal signs are becoming increasing common with type annotations becoming part of best practices (and, as a result, signatures to classes, functions, and methods regularly include spaces around the equal signs). I realize that this will seem alien to many coders, but it is far easier on my eyes.
  2. I use some so-called "power features", primarily dunder methods, to make my interfaces easier to access and use. This is disfavored in the Google Python Style Guide because such code is often more difficult for others to read. To address that concern, I try to document and comment as to what the code is doing whenever I used any of the "power features" of Python.

Because of the first exception, the project does not use a code formatter (such as ruff format), which would remove those spaces.

def apply(self, sections: MutableMapping[str, str]) -> dict[str, Any]:
    """Applies every rule, in order, to `sections`.

    Args:
        sections: the sections of text, by name. Rules that make or change
            sections change it in place.

    Returns:
        The value of each variable, by name. A variable whose rules found
            nothing is False (flags), 0 (counts), an empty `list`
            (matches and names), or None (labels and sections).

    """
    results: dict[str, Any] = {}
    for rule in self.rules:
        rule.apply(sections, results)
    return results

@classmethod
def load(cls, *sources: str | pathlib.Path) -> Rulebook:
    """Loads rules from CSV files.

    Args:
        *sources: names of built-in rulebooks (such as "judges"), or paths
            to CSV files or to folders of them. The rules are applied in
            the order they are given (and, in a folder, in the
            alphabetical order of the files). A file that two sources
            name is read only the first time.

    Returns:
        A rulebook with the rules of every source.

    Raises:
        FileNotFoundError: if a source is not a built-in rulebook or a file
            or folder.
        ValueError: if a file is missing a column or a row is not a valid
            rule. The message names the file and row.

    """
    rules: list[Rule] = []
    names: list[str] = []
    read: set[pathlib.Path] = set()
    for source in sources:
        for path in find_instructions(source):
            if path.resolve() in read:
                continue
            read.add(path.resolve())
            rules.extend(_read(path))
            names.append(path.stem)
    return cls(rules = rules, name = ', '.join(names))

def add_jcs(
    roster: pd.DataFrame,
    folder: pathlib.Path | str | None = None,
    *,
    scores_folder: pathlib.Path | str | None = None,
    martin_quinn: pathlib.Path | str | None = None,
    update: bool = False) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Adds each appointment's Judicial Common Space score as "jcs".

    The scores are computed by `judicial_common_space.compute` from the
    FJC's files in the "raw" folder of `folder` (the files that the roster
    was made from), Voteview's NOMINATE scores, the dates of senators'
    service, Wikipedia's lists of circuit judges' duty stations (if they
    can be downloaded), and the justices' Martin-Quinn scores (if they can
    be found).

    Args:
        roster: a roster with a row for each appointment, as
            `parser.build_roster` makes it.
        folder: the data folder with the FJC's files. Defaults to None, in
            which case `downloader.data_folder()` is used.
        scores_folder: the folder for the other files. Defaults to None, in
            which case the data folder of judicial-common-space is used.
        martin_quinn: the path of the file of the justices' Martin-Quinn
            scores. Defaults to None, in which case the file is downloaded
            if it is not there. Without it, the justices have no score.
        update: whether to download the files again even if they are there.
            Defaults to False.

    Returns:
        A new roster with "jcs" after "senate_vote". It is missing for an
            appointment that has no score (as for one by Herbert Hoover,
            whom Voteview does not score).

    Raises:
        KeyError: if `roster` lacks "nid" or "sequence".

    """
    _require(roster, ['nid', 'sequence'])
    files = jcs.sources.paths(scores_folder)
    files.update(_fjc_files(folder, update = update))
    jcs.sources.download(_POLITICS, scores_folder, overwrite = update)
    try:
        jcs.sources.download(
            'duty_stations', scores_folder, overwrite = update)
    except Exception as error:  # noqa: BLE001
        logger.warning(
            'could not download the duty stations of circuit judges, so '
            'judges whose careers show no state have their birth states: %s',
            error)
    try:
        found = _martin_quinn_file(martin_quinn, scores_folder, update = update)
    except RuntimeError as error:
        logger.warning('%s, so the justices have no scores', error)
        found = None
    scored, _ = jcs.compute(files, martin_quinn = found)
    keyed = scored[['nid', 'sequence', 'jcs']].assign(
        nid = pd.to_numeric(scored['nid']).astype('Int64'),
        sequence = pd.to_numeric(scored['sequence']).astype('Int64'),
        jcs = pd.to_numeric(scored['jcs']).astype('Float64'))
    return _insert(roster, keyed, ['jcs'])

A justice's terms belong to the appointment that the justice served in then, so William Rehnquist's terms as Chief Justice are those of his second appointment (see martin_quinn_terms). The added columns are:

Column Meaning mq_first, mq_last The justice's score in the first and last terms of the appointment. mq_mean The mean of the justice's scores in the terms of the appointment. mq_terms The number of terms of the appointment that are scored.

def add_martin_quinn(
    roster: pd.DataFrame,
    folder: pathlib.Path | str | None = None,
    *,
    scores_folder: pathlib.Path | str | None = None,
    martin_quinn: pathlib.Path | str | None = None,
    update: bool = False,
    terms: pd.DataFrame | None = None) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Adds the Martin-Quinn scores of each appointment to the Supreme Court.

    A justice's terms belong to the appointment that the justice served in
    then, so William Rehnquist's terms as Chief Justice are those of his
    second appointment (see `martin_quinn_terms`). The added columns are:

    | Column | Meaning |
    | --- | --- |
    | `mq_first`, `mq_last` | The justice's score in the first and last terms of the appointment. |
    | `mq_mean` | The mean of the justice's scores in the terms of the appointment. |
    | `mq_terms` | The number of terms of the appointment that are scored. |

    They are missing for every other appointment, and for one with no
    scored terms.

    Args:
        roster: a roster with a row for each appointment, as
            `parser.build_roster` makes it.
        folder: the data folder with the FJC's files. Defaults to None, in
            which case `downloader.data_folder()` is used.
        scores_folder: the folder for the file of Martin-Quinn scores.
            Defaults to None, in which case the data folder of
            judicial-common-space is used.
        martin_quinn: the path of the file of the justices' Martin-Quinn
            scores ("justices.csv"). Defaults to None, in which case the file
            is downloaded if it is not there.
        update: whether to download the files again even if they are there.
            Defaults to False.
        terms: the justices' scores in each term, as `martin_quinn_terms`
            returns them. Defaults to None, in which case they are found
            from the files (and the other arguments are not used).

    Returns:
        A new roster with the columns after "senate_vote" (and "jcs", if it
            is there).

    Raises:
        KeyError: if `roster` lacks "nid" or "sequence".
        RuntimeError: if there is no file of Martin-Quinn scores and it
            cannot be downloaded.

    """
    _require(roster, ['nid', 'sequence'])
    if terms is None:

    service: pd.DataFrame | pathlib.Path | str,
    demographics: pd.DataFrame | pathlib.Path | str,
    career: pd.DataFrame | pathlib.Path | str | None = None,
    *,
    rulebook: rules.Rulebook | pathlib.Path | str = 'judges') -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Makes a table with a row for each court that each judge has served on.

    The table has these columns:

    | Column | Meaning |
    | --- | --- |
    | `nid` | The FJC's number for the judge. |
    | `judge` | The judge's name, as the FJC reports it. |
    | `last_name`, `first_name`, `middle_name`, `suffix` | Its parts. |
    | `name_first_middle_last`, ... | The name written in each of the ways that `names.permutations` writes it, for matching it against other sources: with and without the middle name or its initial and the suffix, and with the letters that the FJC puts in square brackets kept or replaced with a period (see `names`). |
    | `sequence` | The FJC's number for the order of the appointment among the judge's, which identifies it with `nid`. |
    | `court`, `court_type` | The court's name and its type. |
    | `circuit_num` | The number of the court's circuit: its own for a court of appeals (12 for the D.C. Circuit and 13 for the Federal Circuit), or for a district court, that of its state now. Missing for other courts. |
    | `start_date`, `end_date`, `senior_date` | The dates the judge's service on the court began (with a commission or a recess appointment) and ended, and the judge took senior status. `end_date` is missing for a judge who is still serving. |
    | `start_year`, `end_year`, `senior_year` | Their years. |
    | `birth_year` | The year the judge was born. |
    | `president` | The president who appointed the judge. |
    | `party` | That president's party: -1 for Democratic and 1 for Republican. Missing for other parties. |
    | `aba_rating` | The American Bar Association's rating, from 1 (not qualified) to 4 (exceptionally well qualified). Missing if there was none, or it was split ("Qualified/Well Qualified"). |
    | `recess` | Whether the judge first took the seat by a recess appointment. |
    | `senate_vote` | The share of senators who voted to confirm the judge (1 for a voice vote). Missing if the vote is not recorded. |
    | `woman`, `minority` | Whether the judge is a woman, and whether the judge's race or ethnicity is anything other than white. Missing if the FJC does not report it. |

    A judge who was reassigned to another court without a new appointment
    (as when the Eleventh Circuit was divided from the Fifth) keeps the
    president, party, rating, recess appointment, and vote of the judge's
    last appointment.

    If `career` is passed, the judge's professional career is the column
    "career", with each position on its own line, in order. It is the text
    that the rules search, so the fields made from it can be checked
    against it. Each variable that `rulebook` makes from the career (see
    `code_careers`) is a column after it. The "judges" rulebook makes
    "prosecutor", "public_defender", "law_clerk", "supreme_court_clerk",
    "solicitor_general", and "law_professor". "career" is missing for a
    judge with no career in the file.

    Args:
        service: the file of federal judicial service, as a path, the table
            that was read from it, or its tidy table.
        demographics: the file of demographics, in any of those forms.
        career: the file of professional careers, in any of those forms.
            Defaults to None, in which case no careers are coded.
        rulebook: the rules that code the careers: a rulebook, or the name of
            a built-in rulebook or the path of a CSV file. Defaults to
            "judges".

    Returns:
        The table, sorted by judge and then by the order of the judge's
            service.

    Raises:
        KeyError: if a file lacks a column that is needed.
        ValueError: if the file of demographics has more than one row for a
            judge, or a variable of `rulebook` has the name of a column of
            the table.

    """
    served = _table(service)
    _require(served, _SERVICE, 'the file of federal judicial service')
    people = _table(demographics)
    _require(people, _PERSONAL, 'the file of demographics')
    order = ['nid', 'sequence'] if 'sequence' in served.columns else ['nid']
    served = served.sort_values(order, kind = 'stable').reset_index(drop = True)
    # A reassigned judge has "None (reassignment)" in place of a president,
    # so the columns of the appointment are taken from the judge's last row
    # that is not a reassignment.
    reassigned = (
        served['appointing_president'].fillna('').str.startswith('None')
        .to_numpy())
    own = pd.Series(np.arange(len(served)), dtype = 'float64').mask(reassigned)
    source = (
        own.groupby(served['nid'], dropna = False).ffill()
        .fillna(-1).astype(int))
    columns = list(_APPOINTMENT)
    appointed = served[columns].reindex(source.to_numpy())
    appointed.index = served.index
    served[columns] = appointed
    # Each row of a judge's service gets the judge's demographics. A judge
    # who is not in the file of demographics has missing ones.
    personal = served[['nid']].merge(
        people[list(_PERSONAL)], on = 'nid', how = 'left',
        validate = 'many_to_one')
    started = served['commission_date'].fillna(
        served['recess_appointment_date'])
    gender = personal['gender'].map({'Female': True, 'Male': False})
    race = personal['race_or_ethnicity']
    roster = pd.DataFrame({
        'nid': served['nid'],
        'judge': served['judge_name'],
        'last_name': personal['last_name'],
        'first_name': personal['first_name'],
        'middle_name': personal['middle_name'],
        'suffix': personal['suffix'],
        'sequence': (
            served['sequence'] if 'sequence' in served.columns
            else served.groupby('nid').cumcount() + 1).astype('Int64'),
        'court': served['court_name'],
        'court_type': served['court_type'],
        'circuit_num': pd.array(
            [_circuit(kind, court) for kind, court in zip(
                served['court_type'], served['court_name'], strict = True)],
            dtype = 'Int64'),
        'start_date': started,
        'end_date': served['termination_date'],
        'senior_date': served['senior_status_date'],
        'start_year': _year(started),
        'end_year': _year(served['termination_date']),
        'senior_year': _year(served['senior_status_date']),
        'birth_year': personal['birth_year'].astype('Int64'),
        'president': served['appointing_president'],
        'party': served['party_of_appointing_president'].map(
            options._PARTIES).astype('Int64'),
        'aba_rating': served['aba_rating'].map(
            options._ABA_RATINGS).astype('Int64'),
        'recess': served['recess_appointment_date'].notna(),
        'senate_vote': pd.array(
            [_vote_share(kind, votes) for kind, votes in zip(
                served['senate_vote_type'], served['ayes_nays'],
                strict = True)],
            dtype = 'Float64'),
        'woman': gender.astype('boolean'),
        'minority': (race != 'White').astype('boolean').mask(race.isna())})
    roster = names.add_permutations(roster)
    if career is not None:
        positions = _table(career)
        _require(
            positions, ['nid', 'position'], 'the file of professional careers')
        roster['career'] = roster['nid'].map(_histories(positions)).astype(
            'str')
        coded = code_careers(positions, roster['nid'], rulebook = rulebook)
        clashes = [c for c in coded.columns if c in roster.columns]
        if clashes:
            message = (
                f'the rulebook makes {clashes}, which are columns of the '
                f'roster already: rename them in the rulebook')
            raise ValueError(message)
        roster = roster.merge(
            coded, left_on = 'nid', right_index = True, how = 'left')
    return roster

def code_careers(
    career: pd.DataFrame | pathlib.Path | str,
    nids: Iterable[int] | None = None,
    *,
    rulebook: rules.Rulebook | pathlib.Path | str = 'judges') -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Makes fields from judges' professional careers with a rulebook.

    Each judge's positions are put in order, one on each line, as the section
    of text "career", which the rules of `rulebook` search (see `rules`).
    Each variable that the rules make is a field. The "judges" rulebook (in
    fjc_biographies' "instructions" folder) makes a flag for each of six
    kinds of positions: "prosecutor", "public_defender", "law_clerk",
    "supreme_court_clerk", "solicitor_general", and "law_professor".

    Args:
        career: the file of professional careers, as a path, the table that
            was read from it, or its tidy table.
        nids: the numbers of the judges to code. A judge with no career in
            the file gets what the rules make of no text (a flag is False, a
            count is 0, and a label is missing). Defaults to None, in which
            case the judges in `career` are coded.
        rulebook: the rules: a rulebook, or the name of a built-in rulebook
            or the path of a CSV file or a folder of them. Defaults to
            "judges".

    Returns:
        A table with a column for each variable of the rulebook, in order,
            labeled by the judges' numbers ("nid").

    Raises:
        KeyError: if `career` lacks a column that is needed.

    """
    positions = _table(career)
    _require(positions, ['nid', 'position'], 'the file of professional careers')
    book = rules.Rulebook.create(rulebook)
    histories = _histories(positions)
    judges = (
        list(histories.index) if nids is None
        else list(dict.fromkeys(int(nid) for nid in nids)))
    coded = [
        book.apply({'career': histories.get(nid, '')}) for nid in judges]
    return pd.DataFrame(
        coded, index = pd.Index(judges, name = 'nid', dtype = 'Int64'),
        columns = book.variables)

def data_folder() -> pathlib.Path:
    """Returns the folder where the files are kept.

    The folder is the one named by the `FJC_BIOGRAPHIES_DATA_DIR` environment
    variable, if it is set. Otherwise, when fjc_biographies runs from its
    repository, it is `options._DATA_FOLDER`: "data/courts/fjc_biographies"
    two folders above the repository, beside the folder of code projects
    (where courtpy and fjc-idb keep their files as well). When fjc_biographies
    is installed as a package, it is "fjc_biographies" in the user's local
    application data folder on Windows ("%LOCALAPPDATA%"), or in
    "~/.local/share" (or "$XDG_DATA_HOME") on other systems.

    Returns:
        The path of the folder. It is not created.

    """
    named = os.environ.get(options._ENV_DATA)
    if named:
        return pathlib.Path(named).expanduser()
    if (pathlib.Path(__file__).parents[2] / 'pyproject.toml').is_file():
        return options._DATA_FOLDER
    if sys.platform == 'win32':
        base = (
            os.environ.get('LOCALAPPDATA')
            or pathlib.Path.home() / 'AppData' / 'Local')
        return pathlib.Path(base) / 'fjc_biographies'
    base = (
        os.environ.get('XDG_DATA_HOME')
        or pathlib.Path.home() / '.local' / 'share')
    return pathlib.Path(base) / 'fjc_biographies'

def download(
    categories: Iterable[str] | str | None = None,
    folder: pathlib.Path | str | None = None,
    *,
    overwrite: bool = False) -> dict[str, pathlib.Path]:
    """Downloads the FJC's files of the directory.

    A file that was downloaded before is skipped unless `overwrite` is True.
    The FJC adds new judges and corrects its data as it goes, so overwrite
    the files to get the latest data.

    Args:
        categories: the categories to download ("demographics", "service",
            "other_service", "education", "career", and "other_nominations").
            Defaults to None, in which case every category is downloaded.
        folder: the data folder, whose "raw" folder the files are saved in.
            Defaults to None, in which case `data_folder()` is used.
        overwrite: whether to download a file that is already there. Defaults
            to False.

    Returns:
        The path of each file, by its category.

    Raises:
        ValueError: if a category is not one of the FJC's.

    Examples:
        >>> import fjc_biographies
        >>> fjc_biographies.download(['service', 'demographics'])  # doctest: +SKIP

    """
    chosen = _categories(categories)
    raw = raw_folder(folder)
    paths = {}
    for category in chosen:
        path = raw / options._CATEGORIES[category]
        if overwrite or not path.is_file():
            _save(options._FJC_URL + path.name, path)
        else:
            logger.info('Skipped %s, which already exists.', path.name)
        paths[category] = path
    return paths

def export(table: pd.DataFrame, path: pathlib.Path | str) -> pathlib.Path:
    """Saves a table as a CSV file.

    Dates are written as "YYYY-MM-DD", and missing values as blank cells.

    Args:

    return saved

            "nid" and "sequence" are missing for a justice who is not found.

    Raises:
        RuntimeError: if there is no file of Martin-Quinn scores and it
            cannot be downloaded.

    """
    files = _fjc_files(folder, update = update)
    path = _martin_quinn_file(martin_quinn, scores_folder, update = update)
    table = jcs.fjc.appointments(files['service'], files['demographics'])
    terms = jcs.scores.justices(
        jcs.politics.justices(path), table, start_year = 0)
    terms = terms.drop(columns = ['jid'], errors = 'ignore')
    return terms.astype({
        'nid': 'Int64', 'sequence': 'Int64', 'martin_quinn': 'Float64',
        'jcs': 'Float64'}).reset_index(drop = True)

def permutations(
    first: Any,
    middle: Any,
    last: Any,
    suffix: Any = None) -> dict[str, str | None]:
    """Returns each way of writing a judge's name.

    Args:
        first: the first name, such as "R[obert]".
        middle: the middle name or names, such as "Lanier". It may be missing.
        last: the last name, such as "Anderson".
        suffix: the suffix, such as "III". Defaults to None.

            module's documentation). All are None if the name has no first
            or last name.

    first, middle, last, suffix = (
        _text(part) for part in (first, middle, last, suffix))
    if not first and not last:
        return dict.fromkeys(columns())
    found: dict[str, str | None] = {}
    for form, parts in _FORMS.items():
        for with_suffix in (False, True):
            name = f'name_{form}{"_suffix" if with_suffix else ""}'
            for brackets, ending in (('remove', ''), ('period', '_bracket_period')):
                cleaned = {
                    'first': _brackets(first, brackets),
                    'middle': _brackets(middle, brackets),
                    'middle_initial': _initial(_brackets(middle, 'remove')),
                    'last': _brackets(last, brackets)}
                written = ' '.join(
                    cleaned[part] for part in parts if cleaned[part])
                if with_suffix and suffix:
                    written = f'{written}, {suffix}'
                found[f'{name}{ending}'] = written

    """Returns the tidy table of a CSV file of the directory.

    path = pathlib.Path(path).expanduser()

def roster_by_judge(roster: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Returns a roster with one row for each judge.

    A roster made by `build_roster` has a row for each appointment: each
    court that each judge has served on. This is the same information
    organized by judge, as the FJC's own "organized by judge" export is. The
    columns that describe the judge (such as the judge's name, "birth_year",
    "woman", and the fields of the judge's career) are given once.
    "appointments" is how many courts the judge has served on. Then the
    columns that describe an appointment (such as "court", "start_date", and
    "party") are given for each, numbered in the order of the judge's
    service: "court_1", "start_date_1", ..., "court_2", and so on. They are
    missing for a judge with fewer appointments than the most that any
    judge has.

    Args:
        roster: a roster with a row for each appointment, as `build_roster`
            makes it, in the order of each judge's service.

    Returns:
        The roster with a row for each judge, in the order that the judges
            first appear in `roster`.

    Raises:
        KeyError: if `roster` lacks "nid" or "court".

    """
    _require(roster, ['nid', 'court'], 'a roster')
    roster = roster.dropna(subset = ['nid']).reset_index(drop = True)
    fields = [c for c in _BY_APPOINTMENT if c in roster.columns]
    personal = [c for c in roster.columns if c not in _BY_APPOINTMENT]
    judges = roster[personal].drop_duplicates('nid').set_index('nid')
    judges.insert(
        len(judges.columns), 'appointments',
        roster.groupby('nid').size().reindex(judges.index).astype('int64'))
    place = roster.groupby('nid').cumcount() + 1
    # A boolean column gets missing values for the judges with fewer
    # appointments, so it is made one that can have them.
    appointed = roster[fields].astype({
        c: 'boolean' for c in fields if roster[c].dtype == bool})
    # `pivot_table` would aggregate each cell, which loses text and types, so
    # each judge's appointments are unstacked instead.
    indexed = appointed.set_index([roster['nid'], place.rename('place')])
    wide = pd.DataFrame(indexed.unstack('place'))  # noqa: PD010
    numbered = [
        (field, number) for number in range(1, int(place.max() or 0) + 1)
        for field in fields]
    wide = wide.reindex(columns = pd.MultiIndex.from_tuples(numbered))
    wide.columns = [f'{field}_{number}' for field, number in numbered]
    return pd.concat(
        [judges, wide.reindex(judges.index)], axis = 1).reset_index()

def run(
    folder: pathlib.Path | str | None = None,
    *,
    update: bool = False,
    rulebook: rules.Rulebook | pathlib.Path | str = 'judges',
    jcs: bool = False,
    martin_quinn: bool | pathlib.Path | str = False,
    scores_folder: pathlib.Path | str | None = None) -> dict[
        str, pathlib.Path]:
    """Downloads, parses, and exports the FJC's files.

    Args:
        folder: the data folder. Defaults to None, in which case
            `downloader.data_folder()` is used.
        update: whether to download the files again even if they are there,
            to get the judges and corrections since they were downloaded.
            Defaults to False.
        rulebook: the rules that make the roster's fields about judges'
            careers (see `parser.code_careers`). Defaults to "judges".
        jcs: whether to add each appointment's Judicial Common Space score
            (see `scores.add_jcs`). Defaults to False.
        martin_quinn: whether to add the justices' Martin-Quinn scores (see
            `scores.add_martin_quinn`) and export their scores in each term,
            or the path of the file of the scores ("justices.csv"), which is
            also used for the justices' Judicial Common Space scores.
            Defaults to False.
        scores_folder: the folder for the files that the scores come from.
            Defaults to None, in which case the data folder of
            judicial-common-space is used.

    Returns:
        The path of each CSV file that was saved, by its category, the
            paths of the roster as "roster_by_appointment" and
            "roster_by_judge", and with `martin_quinn`, the path of the
            justices' scores in each term as "martin_quinn_terms".

    Examples:
        >>> import fjc_biographies
        >>> fjc_biographies.run(update = True)  # doctest: +SKIP

    """
    root = pathlib.Path(folder).expanduser() if folder else (
        downloader.data_folder())
    tables = parser.load_all(root, update = update)
    roster = parser.build_roster(
        tables['service'], tables['demographics'], tables['career'],
        rulebook = rulebook)
    # A path names the file of Martin-Quinn scores, and True finds it.
    path = None if isinstance(martin_quinn, bool) else martin_quinn
    if jcs:
        roster = scores.add_jcs(
            roster, root, scores_folder = scores_folder, martin_quinn = path,
            update = update)
    terms = None
    if martin_quinn:
        terms = scores.martin_quinn_terms(
            root, scores_folder = scores_folder, martin_quinn = path,
            update = update and not jcs)
        roster = scores.add_martin_quinn(roster, terms = terms)
    tables['roster_by_appointment'] = roster
    tables['roster_by_judge'] = parser.roster_by_judge(roster)
    if terms is not None:
        tables['martin_quinn_terms'] = terms
    return {
        name: export(table, root / f'{name}.csv')
        for name, table in tables.items()}

def tidy(table: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Returns a table of the directory that is easy to use.

    A tidy table is not changed, so a table can be tidied more than once.

    Args:
        table: a table of one of the FJC's files, as it was read.

    Returns:
        A new table whose columns have lower case names, with underscores in
            place of spaces and punctuation (and some shorter names, such as
            "position" for "Professional Career", which are in
            `options._COLUMN_NAMES`). Text has no spaces at its ends, and a
            blank cell is missing. "nid", "jid", "sequence", and the months
            and days of births and deaths are whole numbers, as are the
            years, and the columns whose names end in "_date" are dates.
            The empty, unnamed columns at the end of the file of other
            federal judicial service are left out.

    """
    tidied: dict[str, pd.Series] = {}
    for column in table.columns:
        name = _column_name(column)
        values = table[column]
        if name in _NUMBERS:
            values = _number(values, r'(\d+)')
        elif name in _YEARS:
            values = _number(values, r'(\d{4})')
        elif pd.api.types.is_datetime64_any_dtype(values.dtype):
            pass
        elif name.endswith('_date'):
            values = pd.to_datetime(
                _text(values), format = 'mixed', errors = 'coerce')
        elif not pd.api.types.is_numeric_dtype(values.dtype):
            values = _text(values)
        unnamed = not name or name.startswith('unnamed_')
        if unnamed and values.isna().all():
            continue
        tidied[name] = values
    return pd.DataFrame(tidied, index = table.index)

def data_folder() -> pathlib.Path:
    """Returns the folder where the files are kept.

    The folder is the one named by the `FJC_BIOGRAPHIES_DATA_DIR` environment
    variable, if it is set. Otherwise, when fjc_biographies runs from its
    repository, it is `options._DATA_FOLDER`: "data/courts/fjc_biographies"
    two folders above the repository, beside the folder of code projects
    (where courtpy and fjc-idb keep their files as well). When fjc_biographies
    is installed as a package, it is "fjc_biographies" in the user's local
    application data folder on Windows ("%LOCALAPPDATA%"), or in
    "~/.local/share" (or "$XDG_DATA_HOME") on other systems.

    Returns:
        The path of the folder. It is not created.

    """
    named = os.environ.get(options._ENV_DATA)
    if named:
        return pathlib.Path(named).expanduser()
    if (pathlib.Path(__file__).parents[2] / 'pyproject.toml').is_file():
        return options._DATA_FOLDER
    if sys.platform == 'win32':
        base = (
            os.environ.get('LOCALAPPDATA')
            or pathlib.Path.home() / 'AppData' / 'Local')
        return pathlib.Path(base) / 'fjc_biographies'
    base = (
        os.environ.get('XDG_DATA_HOME')
        or pathlib.Path.home() / '.local' / 'share')
    return pathlib.Path(base) / 'fjc_biographies'

def download(
    categories: Iterable[str] | str | None = None,
    folder: pathlib.Path | str | None = None,
    *,
    overwrite: bool = False) -> dict[str, pathlib.Path]:
    """Downloads the FJC's files of the directory.

    A file that was downloaded before is skipped unless `overwrite` is True.
    The FJC adds new judges and corrects its data as it goes, so overwrite
    the files to get the latest data.

    Args:
        categories: the categories to download ("demographics", "service",
            "other_service", "education", "career", and "other_nominations").
            Defaults to None, in which case every category is downloaded.
        folder: the data folder, whose "raw" folder the files are saved in.
            Defaults to None, in which case `data_folder()` is used.
        overwrite: whether to download a file that is already there. Defaults
            to False.

    Returns:
        The path of each file, by its category.

    Raises:
        ValueError: if a category is not one of the FJC's.

    Examples:
        >>> import fjc_biographies
        >>> fjc_biographies.download(['service', 'demographics'])  # doctest: +SKIP

    """
    chosen = _categories(categories)
    raw = raw_folder(folder)
    paths = {}
    for category in chosen:
        path = raw / options._CATEGORIES[category]
        if overwrite or not path.is_file():
            _save(options._FJC_URL + path.name, path)
        else:
            logger.info('Skipped %s, which already exists.', path.name)
        paths[category] = path
    return paths

def export(table: pd.DataFrame, path: pathlib.Path | str) -> pathlib.Path:
    """Saves a table as a CSV file.

    Dates are written as "YYYY-MM-DD", and missing values as blank cells.

    Args:
        table: the table.
        path: where to save it. Its folder is created if needed.

    tables = parser.load_all(root, update = update)
    roster = parser.build_roster(
        tables['service'], tables['demographics'], tables['career'],
        rulebook = rulebook)

    path = None if isinstance(martin_quinn, bool) else martin_quinn
    if jcs:
        roster = scores.add_jcs(
            roster, root, scores_folder = scores_folder, martin_quinn = path,
            update = update)
    terms = None
    if martin_quinn:
        terms = scores.martin_quinn_terms(
            root, scores_folder = scores_folder, martin_quinn = path,
            update = update and not jcs)
        roster = scores.add_martin_quinn(roster, terms = terms)

    tables['roster_by_judge'] = parser.roster_by_judge(roster)

        tables['martin_quinn_terms'] = terms
    return {
        name: export(table, root / f'{name}.csv')
        for name, table in tables.items()}

docs.text:
Writes judges' names in the ways that other sources may write them.

The FJC gives each judge's name in parts: first, middle, and last names and a suffix (such as "Jr." or "III"). Opinions, other datasets, and news write a judge's name in other ways, so the roster has a column for each way, which can be matched against them:

Column Example name_first_middle_last Robert Lanier Anderson name_first_middle_last_suffix Robert Lanier Anderson, III name_first_middle_initial_last Robert L. Anderson name_first_middle_initial_last_suffix Robert L. Anderson, III name_first_last Robert Anderson name_first_last_suffix Robert Anderson, III

The FJC puts the letters of a name that a judge does not use in square brackets, as in "R[obert] Lanier Anderson III", who went by "R. Lanier Anderson". So each column above has the brackets removed ("Robert"), and a second column, whose name ends in "_bracket_period", has the brackets and the letters in them replaced with a period ("R."):

Column Example name_first_middle_last_bracket_period R. Lanier Anderson name_first_middle_last_suffix_bracket_period R. Lanier Anderson, III ... ...

For a name without brackets, the two columns are the same. A part of a name that is missing is left out, so a judge without a middle name has "Mary Lynch" for both "name_first_middle_last" and "name_first_last", and a judge without a suffix has no comma.

def add_permutations(table: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Adds a column for each way of writing judges' names.

    Args:
        table: a table with the columns "first_name", "middle_name",
            "last_name", and "suffix" (such as a roster or the tidy table of
            the file of demographics).

    Returns:
        A new table with the columns of `permutations` after "suffix".

    Raises:
        KeyError: if `table` lacks one of the parts of a name.

    """
    missing = [part for part in _PARTS if part not in table.columns]
    if missing:
        message = (
            f'names are written from the columns {missing}, which the table '
            f'does not have')
        raise KeyError(message)
    written = pd.DataFrame(
        [permutations(*parts) for parts in zip(
            *(table[part] for part in _PARTS), strict = True)],
        index = table.index, columns = columns(), dtype = 'str')
    place = list(table.columns).index('suffix') + 1
    before, after = table.iloc[:, :place], table.iloc[:, place:]
    return pd.concat([before, written, after], axis = 1)

def permutations(
    first: Any,
    middle: Any,
    last: Any,
    suffix: Any = None) -> dict[str, str | None]:
    """Returns each way of writing a judge's name.

    Args:
        first: the first name, such as "R[obert]".
        middle: the middle name or names, such as "Lanier". It may be missing.
        last: the last name, such as "Anderson".
        suffix: the suffix, such as "III". Defaults to None.

    Returns:
        Each way of writing the name, by the name of its column (see the
            module's documentation). All are None if the name has no first
            or last name.

    """
    first, middle, last, suffix = (
        _text(part) for part in (first, middle, last, suffix))
    if not first and not last:
        return dict.fromkeys(columns())
    found: dict[str, str | None] = {}
    for form, parts in _FORMS.items():
        for with_suffix in (False, True):
            name = f'name_{form}{"_suffix" if with_suffix else ""}'
            for brackets, ending in (('remove', ''), ('period', '_bracket_period')):
                cleaned = {
                    'first': _brackets(first, brackets),
                    'middle': _brackets(middle, brackets),
                    'middle_initial': _initial(_brackets(middle, 'remove')),
                    'last': _brackets(last, brackets)}
                written = ' '.join(
                    cleaned[part] for part in parts if cleaned[part])
                if with_suffix and suffix:
                    written = f'{written}, {suffix}'
                found[f'{name}{ending}'] = written
    return found

docs.text:
Parses the FJC's Biographical Directory of Article III Federal Judges.

Each of the FJC's six files (see downloader) becomes a tidy table with load: its columns get short, lower case names (such as "commission_date" for "Commission Date"), blank cells are missing, the FJC's numbers ("nid", "sequence", and the years) are whole numbers, and its dates are dates.

build_roster combines the files of federal judicial service, demographics, and professional careers into one table, with a row for each court that each judge has served on (each appointment), that codes what researchers usually want to know about a judge's appointment (such as the party of the appointing president and the share of senators who voted to confirm the judge). It is the table that courtpy uses to identify the judges of cases:

import fjc_biographies

tables = fjc_biographies.load_all()
roster = fjc_biographies.build_roster(
    tables['service'], tables['demographics'], tables['career'])
by_judge = fjc_biographies.roster_by_judge(roster)

roster_by_judge organizes the same roster with a row for each judge.

The fields that a roster has about judges' careers are made by a rulebook (see rules): the "judges" rulebook in fjc_biographies' "instructions" folder, unless another is named. It is a CSV file, so fields can be added or changed in a spreadsheet, without changing fjc_biographies.

Contents

build_roster: makes a table with a row for each court that each judge has served on. code_careers: makes fields from judges' professional careers with a rulebook. load: returns the tidy table of one of the FJC's files. load_all: returns the tidy tables of all of the FJC's files. read: returns the tidy table of a CSV file of the directory. roster_by_judge: returns a roster with one row for each judge. tidy: returns a table of the directory with names, missing values, and types that are easy to use.

def build_roster(
    service: pd.DataFrame | pathlib.Path | str,
    demographics: pd.DataFrame | pathlib.Path | str,
    career: pd.DataFrame | pathlib.Path | str | None = None,
    *,
    rulebook: rules.Rulebook | pathlib.Path | str = 'judges') -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Makes a table with a row for each court that each judge has served on.

    The table has these columns:

    | Column | Meaning |
    | --- | --- |
    | `nid` | The FJC's number for the judge. |
    | `judge` | The judge's name, as the FJC reports it. |
    | `last_name`, `first_name`, `middle_name`, `suffix` | Its parts. |
    | `name_first_middle_last`, ... | The name written in each of the ways that `names.permutations` writes it, for matching it against other sources: with and without the middle name or its initial and the suffix, and with the letters that the FJC puts in square brackets kept or replaced with a period (see `names`). |
    | `sequence` | The FJC's number for the order of the appointment among the judge's, which identifies it with `nid`. |
    | `court`, `court_type` | The court's name and its type. |
    | `circuit_num` | The number of the court's circuit: its own for a court of appeals (12 for the D.C. Circuit and 13 for the Federal Circuit), or for a district court, that of its state now. Missing for other courts. |
    | `start_date`, `end_date`, `senior_date` | The dates the judge's service on the court began (with a commission or a recess appointment) and ended, and the judge took senior status. `end_date` is missing for a judge who is still serving. |
    | `start_year`, `end_year`, `senior_year` | Their years. |
    | `birth_year` | The year the judge was born. |
    | `president` | The president who appointed the judge. |
    | `party` | That president's party: -1 for Democratic and 1 for Republican. Missing for other parties. |
    | `aba_rating` | The American Bar Association's rating, from 1 (not qualified) to 4 (exceptionally well qualified). Missing if there was none, or it was split ("Qualified/Well Qualified"). |
    | `recess` | Whether the judge first took the seat by a recess appointment. |
    | `senate_vote` | The share of senators who voted to confirm the judge (1 for a voice vote). Missing if the vote is not recorded. |
    | `woman`, `minority` | Whether the judge is a woman, and whether the judge's race or ethnicity is anything other than white. Missing if the FJC does not report it. |

    A judge who was reassigned to another court without a new appointment
    (as when the Eleventh Circuit was divided from the Fifth) keeps the
    president, party, rating, recess appointment, and vote of the judge's
    last appointment.

    If `career` is passed, the judge's professional career is the column
    "career", with each position on its own line, in order. It is the text
    that the rules search, so the fields made from it can be checked
    against it. Each variable that `rulebook` makes from the career (see
    `code_careers`) is a column after it. The "judges" rulebook makes
    "prosecutor", "public_defender", "law_clerk", "supreme_court_clerk",
    "solicitor_general", and "law_professor". "career" is missing for a
    judge with no career in the file.

    Args:
        service: the file of federal judicial service, as a path, the table
            that was read from it, or its tidy table.
        demographics: the file of demographics, in any of those forms.
        career: the file of professional careers, in any of those forms.
            Defaults to None, in which case no careers are coded.
        rulebook: the rules that code the careers: a rulebook, or the name of
            a built-in rulebook or the path of a CSV file. Defaults to
            "judges".

    Returns:
        The table, sorted by judge and then by the order of the judge's
            service.

    Raises:
        KeyError: if a file lacks a column that is needed.
        ValueError: if the file of demographics has more than one row for a
            judge, or a variable of `rulebook` has the name of a column of
            the table.

    """
    served = _table(service)
    _require(served, _SERVICE, 'the file of federal judicial service')
    people = _table(demographics)
    _require(people, _PERSONAL, 'the file of demographics')
    order = ['nid', 'sequence'] if 'sequence' in served.columns else ['nid']
    served = served.sort_values(order, kind = 'stable').reset_index(drop = True)
    # A reassigned judge has "None (reassignment)" in place of a president,
    # so the columns of the appointment are taken from the judge's last row
    # that is not a reassignment.
    reassigned = (
        served['appointing_president'].fillna('').str.startswith('None')
        .to_numpy())
    own = pd.Series(np.arange(len(served)), dtype = 'float64').mask(reassigned)
    source = (
        own.groupby(served['nid'], dropna = False).ffill()
        .fillna(-1).astype(int))
    columns = list(_APPOINTMENT)
    appointed = served[columns].reindex(source.to_numpy())
    appointed.index = served.index
    served[columns] = appointed
    # Each row of a judge's service gets the judge's demographics. A judge
    # who is not in the file of demographics has missing ones.
    personal = served[['nid']].merge(
        people[list(_PERSONAL)], on = 'nid', how = 'left',
        validate = 'many_to_one')
    started = served['commission_date'].fillna(
        served['recess_appointment_date'])
    gender = personal['gender'].map({'Female': True, 'Male': False})
    race = personal['race_or_ethnicity']
    roster = pd.DataFrame({
        'nid': served['nid'],
        'judge': served['judge_name'],
        'last_name': personal['last_name'],
        'first_name': personal['first_name'],
        'middle_name': personal['middle_name'],
        'suffix': personal['suffix'],
        'sequence': (
            served['sequence'] if 'sequence' in served.columns
            else served.groupby('nid').cumcount() + 1).astype('Int64'),
        'court': served['court_name'],
        'court_type': served['court_type'],
        'circuit_num': pd.array(
            [_circuit(kind, court) for kind, court in zip(
                served['court_type'], served['court_name'], strict = True)],
            dtype = 'Int64'),
        'start_date': started,
        'end_date': served['termination_date'],
        'senior_date': served['senior_status_date'],
        'start_year': _year(started),
        'end_year': _year(served['termination_date']),
        'senior_year': _year(served['senior_status_date']),
        'birth_year': personal['birth_year'].astype('Int64'),
        'president': served['appointing_president'],
        'party': served['party_of_appointing_president'].map(
            options._PARTIES).astype('Int64'),
        'aba_rating': served['aba_rating'].map(
            options._ABA_RATINGS).astype('Int64'),
        'recess': served['recess_appointment_date'].notna(),
        'senate_vote': pd.array(
            [_vote_share(kind, votes) for kind, votes in zip(
                served['senate_vote_type'], served['ayes_nays'],
                strict = True)],
            dtype = 'Float64'),
        'woman': gender.astype('boolean'),
        'minority': (race != 'White').astype('boolean').mask(race.isna())})
    roster = names.add_permutations(roster)
    if career is not None:
        positions = _table(career)
        _require(
            positions, ['nid', 'position'], 'the file of professional careers')
        roster['career'] = roster['nid'].map(_histories(positions)).astype(
            'str')
        coded = code_careers(positions, roster['nid'], rulebook = rulebook)
        clashes = [c for c in coded.columns if c in roster.columns]
        if clashes:
            message = (
                f'the rulebook makes {clashes}, which are columns of the '
                f'roster already: rename them in the rulebook')
            raise ValueError(message)
        roster = roster.merge(
            coded, left_on = 'nid', right_index = True, how = 'left')
    return roster

def code_careers(
    career: pd.DataFrame | pathlib.Path | str,
    nids: Iterable[int] | None = None,
    *,
    rulebook: rules.Rulebook | pathlib.Path | str = 'judges') -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Makes fields from judges' professional careers with a rulebook.

    Each judge's positions are put in order, one on each line, as the section
    of text "career", which the rules of `rulebook` search (see `rules`).
    Each variable that the rules make is a field. The "judges" rulebook (in
    fjc_biographies' "instructions" folder) makes a flag for each of six
    kinds of positions: "prosecutor", "public_defender", "law_clerk",
    "supreme_court_clerk", "solicitor_general", and "law_professor".

    Args:
        career: the file of professional careers, as a path, the table that
            was read from it, or its tidy table.
        nids: the numbers of the judges to code. A judge with no career in
            the file gets what the rules make of no text (a flag is False, a
            count is 0, and a label is missing). Defaults to None, in which
            case the judges in `career` are coded.
        rulebook: the rules: a rulebook, or the name of a built-in rulebook
            or the path of a CSV file or a folder of them. Defaults to
            "judges".

    Returns:
        A table with a column for each variable of the rulebook, in order,
            labeled by the judges' numbers ("nid").

    Raises:
        KeyError: if `career` lacks a column that is needed.

    """
    positions = _table(career)
    _require(positions, ['nid', 'position'], 'the file of professional careers')
    book = rules.Rulebook.create(rulebook)
    histories = _histories(positions)
    judges = (
        list(histories.index) if nids is None
        else list(dict.fromkeys(int(nid) for nid in nids)))
    coded = [
        book.apply({'career': histories.get(nid, '')}) for nid in judges]
    return pd.DataFrame(
        coded, index = pd.Index(judges, name = 'nid', dtype = 'Int64'),
        columns = book.variables)

def read(path: pathlib.Path | str, **kwargs: Any) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Returns the tidy table of a CSV file of the directory.

    The FJC's files are in UTF-8, but a file that was saved again by a
    spreadsheet may be in Windows-1252, which is read too.

    Args:
        path: the path of the file, which may begin with "~" for the user's
            home folder.
        **kwargs: arguments for `pandas.read_csv`.

    Returns:
        The table (see `tidy`).

    """
    path = pathlib.Path(path).expanduser()
    settings: dict[str, Any] = {
        'dtype': str, 'keep_default_na': False, **kwargs}
    try:
        table = pd.read_csv(path, encoding = 'utf-8-sig', **settings)
    except UnicodeDecodeError:
        table = pd.read_csv(path, encoding = 'cp1252', **settings)
    return tidy(table)

def roster_by_judge(roster: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Returns a roster with one row for each judge.

    A roster made by `build_roster` has a row for each appointment: each
    court that each judge has served on. This is the same information
    organized by judge, as the FJC's own "organized by judge" export is. The
    columns that describe the judge (such as the judge's name, "birth_year",
    "woman", and the fields of the judge's career) are given once.
    "appointments" is how many courts the judge has served on. Then the
    columns that describe an appointment (such as "court", "start_date", and
    "party") are given for each, numbered in the order of the judge's
    service: "court_1", "start_date_1", ..., "court_2", and so on. They are
    missing for a judge with fewer appointments than the most that any
    judge has.

    Args:
        roster: a roster with a row for each appointment, as `build_roster`
            makes it, in the order of each judge's service.

    Returns:
        The roster with a row for each judge, in the order that the judges
            first appear in `roster`.

    Raises:
        KeyError: if `roster` lacks "nid" or "court".

    """
    _require(roster, ['nid', 'court'], 'a roster')
    roster = roster.dropna(subset = ['nid']).reset_index(drop = True)
    fields = [c for c in _BY_APPOINTMENT if c in roster.columns]
    personal = [c for c in roster.columns if c not in _BY_APPOINTMENT]
    judges = roster[personal].drop_duplicates('nid').set_index('nid')
    judges.insert(
        len(judges.columns), 'appointments',
        roster.groupby('nid').size().reindex(judges.index).astype('int64'))
    place = roster.groupby('nid').cumcount() + 1
    # A boolean column gets missing values for the judges with fewer
    # appointments, so it is made one that can have them.
    appointed = roster[fields].astype({
        c: 'boolean' for c in fields if roster[c].dtype == bool})
    # `pivot_table` would aggregate each cell, which loses text and types, so
    # each judge's appointments are unstacked instead.
    indexed = appointed.set_index([roster['nid'], place.rename('place')])
    wide = pd.DataFrame(indexed.unstack('place'))  # noqa: PD010
    numbered = [
        (field, number) for number in range(1, int(place.max() or 0) + 1)
        for field in fields]
    wide = wide.reindex(columns = pd.MultiIndex.from_tuples(numbered))
    wide.columns = [f'{field}_{number}' for field, number in numbered]
    return pd.concat(
        [judges, wide.reindex(judges.index)], axis = 1).reset_index()

def tidy(table: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Returns a table of the directory that is easy to use.

    A tidy table is not changed, so a table can be tidied more than once.

    Args:
        table: a table of one of the FJC's files, as it was read.

    Returns:
        A new table whose columns have lower case names, with underscores in
            place of spaces and punctuation (and some shorter names, such as
            "position" for "Professional Career", which are in
            `options._COLUMN_NAMES`). Text has no spaces at its ends, and a
            blank cell is missing. "nid", "jid", "sequence", and the months
            and days of births and deaths are whole numbers, as are the
            years, and the columns whose names end in "_date" are dates.
            The empty, unnamed columns at the end of the file of other
            federal judicial service are left out.

    """
    tidied: dict[str, pd.Series] = {}
    for column in table.columns:
        name = _column_name(column)
        values = table[column]
        if name in _NUMBERS:
            values = _number(values, r'(\d+)')
        elif name in _YEARS:
            values = _number(values, r'(\d{4})')
        elif pd.api.types.is_datetime64_any_dtype(values.dtype):
            pass
        elif name.endswith('_date'):
            values = pd.to_datetime(
                _text(values), format = 'mixed', errors = 'coerce')
        elif not pd.api.types.is_numeric_dtype(values.dtype):
            values = _text(values)
        unnamed = not name or name.startswith('unnamed_')
        if unnamed and values.isna().all():
            continue
        tidied[name] = values
    return pd.DataFrame(tidied, index = table.index)

docs.text:
Rules that make new fields from the text of judges' biographies.

The rules are written in CSV files (spreadsheets), so they can be read and changed without knowing Python. They are the rules of courtpy, whose "judges" rulebook (in fjc_biographies' "instructions" folder) codes each judge's professional career. Each row is one rule. The columns are:

Column Meaning target The section of text to search, such as "career". Several sections can be listed, separated by commas, and are searched in order. variable The name of the column that the rule makes (or adds to). kind What the rule does (see below). pattern A regular expression to search for. value For a label rule, the value to record. Otherwise blank. ignorecase TRUE to ignore the difference between capital and lower-case letters. dotall TRUE for "." in the pattern to also match line breaks. note Anything you want to say about the rule. It is not used.

The kinds of rules:

Kind Makes flag TRUE if the pattern appears, and otherwise FALSE. count The number of times the pattern appears. matches A list of every match. label The rule's value if the pattern appears. The first rule for a variable that matches wins, so it can turn text into categories (such as kinds of positions into numbers). names A list of names, found by splitting the text wherever the pattern matches. The pattern should match the words and punctuation between names. section A new section of text: the first match. Later rules can search it. excerpts A new section of text: every match, one per line. split Two new sections, named in variable (such as "before, after"): the text before and after the first match. remove Nothing. It deletes every match from the target for the rules after it.

Rules are applied from top to bottom, so a rule can search a section made by a rule above it. Rules with the same variable are combined: flags are TRUE if any rule matches, counts are added, lists of matches and names are joined, and the first label or section that matches is used.

Contents

Kinds

the kinds of rules. Rule: one rule from a CSV file. Rulebook: an ordered collection of rules. find_instructions: returns the CSV files for a built-in or custom rulebook. split_names: splits text into names wherever a pattern matches.

def apply(
    self,
    sections: MutableMapping[str, str],
    results: MutableMapping[str, Any]) -> None:
    """Applies the rule to `sections`, recording what it finds in `results`.

    Args:
        sections: the sections of text, by name. `remove`, `section`,
            `excerpts`, and `split` rules change it.
        results: the variables found so far, by name. It is changed in
            place.

    """
    texts = [sections[t] for t in self.targets if sections.get(t)]
    if self.kind == 'remove':
        for target in self.targets:
            if sections.get(target):
                sections[target] = self.pattern.sub(' ', sections[target])
    elif self.kind == 'split':
        self._split(texts, sections, results)
    elif self.kind == 'flag':
        flagged = any(self.pattern.search(text) for text in texts)
        results[self.variable] = bool(results.get(self.variable)) or flagged
    elif self.kind == 'count':
        counted = sum(
            1 for text in texts for _ in self.pattern.finditer(text))
        results[self.variable] = results.get(self.variable, 0) + counted
    elif self.kind == 'matches':
        matches = results.setdefault(self.variable, [])
        matches.extend(
            m.group(0).strip() for t in texts
            for m in self.pattern.finditer(t))
    elif self.kind == 'label':
        if results.get(self.variable) is None:
            matched = any(self.pattern.search(text) for text in texts)
            results[self.variable] = self.value if matched else None
    elif self.kind == 'names':
        names = results.setdefault(self.variable, [])
        for text in texts:
            names.extend(n for n in split_names(text, self.pattern)
                         if n not in names)
    elif self.kind == 'section':
        if not results.get(self.variable):
            match = next(
                (m for t in texts if (m := self.pattern.search(t))), None)
            section = match.group(0).strip() if match else None
            results[self.variable] = section
            if section:
                sections[self.variable] = section
    elif self.kind == 'excerpts':
        excerpts = [
            m.group(0).strip() for t in texts
            for m in self.pattern.finditer(t) if m.group(0).strip()]
        existing = results.get(self.variable)
        joined = '\n'.join(([existing] if existing else []) + excerpts)
        results[self.variable] = joined or None
        if joined:
            sections[self.variable] = joined

@classmethod
def create(cls, row: Mapping[str, Any]) -> Rule:
    """Returns a rule made from a row of a CSV file.

    Args:
        row: the cells of the row, by the names of the columns.

    Returns:
        The rule.

    Raises:
        ValueError: if the kind is not one of `KINDS`, the pattern is not
            a valid regular expression, a cell that is needed is blank, or
            a `split` rule does not name two variables.

    """
    kind = str(row.get('kind') or '').strip().lower()
    if kind not in KINDS:
        message = f'the kind {kind!r} is not one of {list(KINDS)}'
        raise ValueError(message)
    targets = tuple(_listify(row.get('target')))
    variables = tuple(_listify(row.get('variable')))
    if not targets:
        message = 'the target is blank'
        raise ValueError(message)
    if kind == 'split' and len(variables) != 2:
        message = (
            'a split rule needs two variables, separated by a comma (such '
            'as "before, after")'
        )
        raise ValueError(message)
    if kind != 'remove' and not variables:
        message = 'the variable is blank'
        raise ValueError(message)
    source = str(row.get('pattern') or '')
    if not source:
        message = 'the pattern is blank'
        raise ValueError(message)
    flags = 0
    if _to_bool(row.get('ignorecase')):
        flags |= re.IGNORECASE
    if _to_bool(row.get('dotall')):
        flags |= re.DOTALL
    try:
        pattern = re.compile(source, flags)
    except re.error as error:
        message = f'the pattern {source!r} is not valid: {error}'
        raise ValueError(message) from error
    value = row.get('value')
    return cls(
        targets = targets,
        variables = variables,
        kind = kind,
        pattern = pattern,
        value = _convert(value) if kind == 'label' else None,
        note = str(row.get('note') or ''))

def apply(self, sections: MutableMapping[str, str]) -> dict[str, Any]:
    """Applies every rule, in order, to `sections`.

    Args:
        sections: the sections of text, by name. Rules that make or change
            sections change it in place.

            nothing is False (flags), 0 (counts), an empty `list`
            (matches and names), or None (labels and sections).

    results: dict[str, Any] = {}
    for rule in self.rules:
        rule.apply(sections, results)
    return results

@classmethod
def load(cls, *sources: str | pathlib.Path) -> Rulebook:
    """Loads rules from CSV files.

    Args:
        *sources: names of built-in rulebooks (such as "judges"), or paths
            to CSV files or to folders of them. The rules are applied in
            the order they are given (and, in a folder, in the
            alphabetical order of the files). A file that two sources
            name is read only the first time.

    Returns:
        A rulebook with the rules of every source.

    Raises:
        FileNotFoundError: if a source is not a built-in rulebook or a file
            or folder.
        ValueError: if a file is missing a column or a row is not a valid
            rule. The message names the file and row.

    """
    rules: list[Rule] = []
    names: list[str] = []
    read: set[pathlib.Path] = set()
    for source in sources:
        for path in find_instructions(source):
            if path.resolve() in read:
                continue
            read.add(path.resolve())
            rules.extend(_read(path))
            names.append(path.stem)
    return cls(rules = rules, name = ', '.join(names))

def find_instructions(source: str | pathlib.Path) -> list[pathlib.Path]:
    """Returns the CSV files for a built-in or custom rulebook.

    Args:
        source: the name of a built-in rulebook (a file in fjc_biographies'
            "instructions" folder, such as "judges"), or the path to a CSV
            file or a folder of them.

    Returns:
        The paths of the CSV files, in the order they are applied.

    Raises:
        FileNotFoundError: if `source` is not a built-in rulebook, a CSV file,
            or a folder with CSV files.

    """
    path = pathlib.Path(source)
    if not path.exists():
        folder = pathlib.Path(
            str(importlib.resources.files('fjc_biographies'))) / 'instructions'
        name = str(source)
        for candidate in (folder / name, folder / f'{name}.csv'):
            if candidate.exists():
                path = candidate
                break
        else:
            built_in = sorted(p.stem for p in folder.glob('*.csv'))
            message = (
                f'{source!r} is not a CSV file, a folder, or a built-in '
                f'rulebook ({built_in})'
            )
            raise FileNotFoundError(message)
    if path.is_dir():
        files = sorted(path.glob('*.csv'))
        if not files:
            message = f'there are no CSV files in {path}'
            raise FileNotFoundError(message)
        return files
    return [path]

def split_names(text: str, separators: re.Pattern[str]) -> list[str]:
    """Splits `text` into names wherever `separators` matches.

    The text is made upper-case and periods and apostrophes are removed first
    (so "O'Scannlain" becomes "OSCANNLAIN"), and line breaks always separate
    names. Pieces without at least two letters are dropped.

    Args:
        text: text with names, such as "Hon. SMITH, JONES, and BROWN".
        separators: a pattern that matches the words and punctuation between
            the names. It is matched against the upper-case text.

    Returns:
        The names, in order, without repeats.

    """
    cleaned = _PUNCTUATION.sub('', text.upper())
    names: list[str] = []
    for line in cleaned.splitlines():
        # The text between matches is used (rather than `re.split`) so that
        # groups in the pattern are not mistaken for names.
        pieces, start = [], 0
        for match in separators.finditer(line):
            pieces.append(line[start:match.start()])
            start = match.end()
        pieces.append(line[start:])
        for piece in pieces:
            name = ' '.join(piece.split())
            if sum(c.isalpha() for c in name) >= 2 and name not in names:
                names.append(name)
    return names

docs.text:
Adds scores of judges' ideology to a roster.

Two kinds of scores can be added to a roster made by parser.build_roster:

  • add_jcs adds each appointment's Judicial Common Space score ("jcs"), computed by the judicial-common-space package (Epstein, Martin, Segal, and Westerland, "The Judicial Common Space," 23 J.L. Econ. & Org. 303 (2007)): the NOMINATE score of the judge's home-state senators of the president's party, or else of the president, and for a justice, the justice's Martin-Quinn score in the first term of the appointment, put on the same scale.
  • add_martin_quinn adds the Martin-Quinn scores of the justices of the Supreme Court, which are estimated from their votes in each term (https://mqscores.wustl.edu): for each appointment to the Supreme Court, the scores of its first and last terms, their mean, and the number of terms. martin_quinn_terms returns every justice's score in every term.

The scores come from files that are downloaded when they are needed, into the data folder of judicial-common-space (see judicial_common_space.utilities.data_folder, which the JUDICIAL_COMMON_SPACE_DATA_DIR environment variable can set, so that courtpy and judicial-common-space share the downloads). The Martin-Quinn website sometimes refuses or fails to answer automated requests. Then save "justices.csv" from https://mqscores.wustl.edu/measures.php in a browser and pass its path as martin_quinn.

Contents

add_jcs: adds each appointment's Judicial Common Space score. add_martin_quinn: adds the Martin-Quinn scores of each appointment to the Supreme Court. martin_quinn_terms: returns each justice's Martin-Quinn score in each term.
